questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the supermajority the Senate must reach to ratify a treaty
questions.stem: Ticket QF-118: a teammate claims the Senate can ratify a treaty with a simple majority. Which rule actually governs ratification?

options.text: Two thirds of the senators present and voting must agree before the Senate ratifies a treaty.
A simple majority is enough once the president has signed the agreement.
options.misconception: believes the president's signature completes ratification

options.text: The House must clear the treaty by two thirds before the Senate debates it.
options.misconception: thinks the House must approve treaties first

options.text: Ratification takes effect only after a majority of the state legislatures concur.
options.misconception: confuses treaty ratification with state conventions

questions.explanation: The Constitution requires two thirds of senators present and voting to ratify a treaty. A simple majority plus presidential signature does not substitute for that supermajority, and the House has no approval role in ratification.
questions.hint: Count the votes the Constitution names, not a bare majority.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the power to declare war from the power to command troops

stimulus.body: Priya wrote in the sprint retro that the president may send troops into a new war whenever he judges it necessary, and that Congress only supplies money afterwards. She called this the commander in chief power doing its job.

questions.stem: Sprint retro thread: Priya claimed the president may order troops into a new war without Congress. Which constitutional idea does that claim miss?

options.text: The president may start a war whenever Congress is out of session and cannot convene.
options.misconception: assumes the president leads in war with no legal limit

options.text: Only Congress may declare war, which separates starting a war from leading the troops.
Once war is declared, all war powers pass to the president and away from Congress.
options.misconception: believes war powers move fully to the executive

options.text: Congress may declare war only if the president agrees in writing beforehand.
options.misconception: thinks the president must approve any declaration

questions.explanation: The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war while the president serves as commander in chief of the armed forces. Priya's claim collapses those two roles and lets the president start wars without any declaration.
questions.hint: Separate who starts the war from who leads the troops.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Speaker of the House holds no veto power
questions.stem: Design review comment: the team wrote that the Speaker of the House may veto a bill the House already passed. Why is that reasoning flawed?

options.text: The Speaker may veto a House bill only if a majority of members support the veto.
options.misconception: treats the Speaker as an executive style veto holder

options.text: The Speaker may veto a bill but only after the Senate has already approved it.
options.misconception: mixes the presidential veto into the Speaker's role

options.text: The Speaker is not an executive official and cannot veto anything at all.
The Speaker's veto is genuine but disappears when the House votes again.
options.misconception: believes the House can overrule its own Speaker

questions.explanation: The veto power belongs to the president, not to the Speaker of the House. The Speaker's constitutional duties are limited to presiding, scheduling, and sending passed bills to the Senate, so a Speaker veto cannot exist.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe what the Senate's rule for ending debate accomplishes
questions.stem: Standup notes ask the team to explain why the Senate's debate rule lets a small group end discussion of a bill.

answer.exemplar: The Senate's standing rule lets a specified number of senators end debate and move to a final vote on the measure, so a bill that minority members have held off the floor can still reach the Senate for a vote. The rule therefore limits how long discussion can be stalled without deciding whether the bill itself should pass.

questions.explanation: The rule is a scheduling tool, and the number needed to invoke it has been reduced over time. What it changes is when the Senate votes, not how the vote comes out, so calling it a veto over the bill is wrong.
questions.hint: Think schedule, not outcome.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what happens when the two chambers pass different bill texts
questions.stem: Refactor request RR-42 asks what happens when the House and Senate pass different versions of the same spending bill.

options.text: The bill becomes law as soon as the chamber with the larger majority approves it.
options.misconception: assumes one chamber's passage is enough to enact

options.text: The bill goes to a conference committee that reconciles the two versions before a final vote.
The president picks whichever version he prefers and signs that version.
options.misconception: believes the president chooses between chamber texts

options.text: Both chambers must pass one shared bill or the spending measure lapses for the year.
options.misconception: misses the conference committee step entirely

questions.explanation: When the chambers approve different versions of the same bill, a conference committee reconciles them and each chamber votes again. Without that agreement no single text reaches the president, which is a common source of gridlock.
questions.hint: Think about the step between two different texts.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why an executive order cannot override a statute

stimulus.body: Version 2.0 will let customers request instant waivers of federal tax obligations. The feature relies only on a signed order from the president, so no legislative vote is needed before the waiver applies.

questions.stem: Release notes question: the product brief promises 'instant tax waivers' issued only by the president. What limits that promise?

options.text: Executive orders carry the same force as statutes once published in the Federal Register.
options.misconception: confuses publication with congressional approval

options.text: The order works until the next congressional recess, when it must be renewed.
options.misconception: invents an expiration rule that does not exist

options.text: A statute or a constitutional limit cannot be overridden by an executive order alone.
Only a unanimous Senate vote can validate an order that touches taxation.
options.misconception: overstates the approval needed for executive orders

questions.explanation: An executive order is a tool for carrying out existing law; it cannot rewrite a statute or override the Constitution. Tax rules must come from Congress, so a president-only waiver scheme cannot legally take effect.
questions.hint: Orders carry out law, they do not replace it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a valid federal statute is not the final word in every dispute
questions.stem: Architecture review note: the team treats a federal statute as the last word in every dispute. Why is that model incomplete?

options.text: Federal statutes apply only in the states that have adopted them by referendum.
options.misconception: believes federal law needs state adoption to apply

options.text: Any state court may interpret federal law differently whenever it disagrees.
options.misconception: grants state courts power to overrule federal law

options.text: A federal statute loses force whenever a state legislature passes a conflicting rule.
options.misconception: reverses the priority between federal and state law

options.text: Courts can invalidate a law, and states may set their own rules where federal law is silent.

questions.explanation: Federal supremacy means valid federal law overrides conflicting state rules, but a federal statute cannot itself violate the Constitution, which courts review. States remain free to legislate in areas that federal law has not occupied.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how two chambers slow the lawmaking process
questions.stem: Incident report asks why most enacted bills had to clear two separate chambers before becoming law.

options.text: Bicameralism forces each bill through two independent chambers, which slows lawmaking.
The two chambers must agree on a committee report before any bill can be debated.
options.misconception: describes conference committees as a debate precondition

options.misconception: restricts bicameralism to spending measures

options.text: Each chamber must vote twice on any bill before the president sees it.
options.misconception: believes every bill needs two rounds in one house

questions.learningObjective: State which chamber may originate a bill raising revenue
questions.stem: Planning note asks the team to describe why a revenue measure must begin in the House rather than the Senate.

answer.exemplar: Article I places the power to originate revenue bills in the House of Representatives. The Senate may amend or reject such a bill but may not originate one, so every revenue measure must first be introduced and passed in the House before the Senate can act on it at all.

questions.explanation: The origination clause is a structural check: the chamber closest to the people must start bills that raise money. The Senate can still amend or block a revenue bill, so the rule constrains the starting point rather than the outcome.
questions.hint: Which chamber is closest to the people?

options.text: Impeachment of a federal judge, which requires two thirds of senators to convict.
options.misconception: confuses impeachment's two thirds rule with treaties

options.text: Override of a presidential veto, which needs two thirds of each chamber to prevail.
options.misconception: treats the veto override as a treaty-style requirement

Confirmation of a Cabinet official, which requires two thirds of senators present.

questions.hint: Three powers use supermajorities, only one is a treaty.

options.misconception: assigns the commander role to Congress instead

options.misconception: believes war powers were reserved to the states

options.misconception: accepts a single office holding both war powers

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the Speaker's duty to send bills from a veto power
questions.stem: Retrospective ticket RS-14 asks why the Speaker's power to send a bill to the Senate is not a veto power.

options.text: Sending a bill onward is a duty and a timing choice, while a veto must be a refusal to sign.
The Speaker does hold a veto, but it disappears once two thirds of the House votes again.
options.misconception: invents a revocable Speaker veto

options.misconception: overstates the Senate's dependence on the Speaker

options.misconception: treats the scheduling power as a budget veto

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish ending debate in the Senate from defeating a bill
questions.stem: Knowledge share prompt asks the team to explain how ending debate differs from defeating a bill.

answer.exemplar: Ending debate only changes what happens next on the Senate floor: once the required number of senators votes to end discussion, the measure moves to a final vote. Defeating a bill is what happens when that final vote fails, so a measure can clear the debate hurdle and still be rejected by the senators.

questions.explanation: Ending debate is a scheduling decision taken by a specified number of senators; it does not decide the bill's fate. The bill's fate is settled by the later final vote, and the two steps are often confused in fast reporting.
questions.hint: One step changes the calendar, the other settles the bill.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the revenue origination rule
questions.stem: Onboarding task asks the team to explain the origin rule that keeps revenue bills starting in the lower chamber.

answer.exemplar: Article I says that all bills for raising revenue must originate in the House of Representatives, not in the Senate. questions.explanation: The rule reserves the introduction of tax and spending bills to the House. It does not strip the Senate of influence, since the Senate may amend or refuse such bills before anything is enacted.
questions.hint: Starting point, not final say.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a judicial nominee can face long delays
questions.stem: Timeline item TL-12 asks why a confirmed judicial nominee has faced long delays before a vote.

options.text: Because a nomination must clear the Senate, which can delay or decline to act on the report.
Because the House must confirm every judicial nominee before the Senate considers it.
options.misconception: adds a House confirmation step for judges

options.text: Because the president may withdraw a nomination at any point in the process.
options.misconception: treats withdrawal as a delay mechanism

options.text: Because nominations must be filed with the Supreme Court for scheduling purposes.
options.misconception: routes nominations through the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: Nominations are confirmed by the Senate, and the Senate's own rules allow consideration to be delayed or set aside. That procedural leverage is why a qualified nominee can wait a long time for a floor vote.
questions.hint: One chamber's rules can hold up consideration.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the historical rationale for the revenue origination rule
questions.stem: Documentation task asks the team to explain why the revenue origination rule was written into the original Constitution.

answer.exemplar: The framers placed the power to originate revenue bills in the House because it was the chamber elected most directly by the people, and revenue was one of the areas where they distrusted legislatures to act without limits. The Senate could still amend or reject such bills, which kept the check without giving up the revenue power entirely.

questions.explanation: The rule was a popular-sovereignty choice for the power to tax and spend. It restrains one chamber's ability to start money bills without removing either chamber's ability to block or amend them.
questions.hint: Which chamber had the strongest claim to legitimacy?

questions.learningObjective: State the votes required to approve a negotiated treaty
questions.stem: Compliance item CM-16 asks which votes are needed to approve a treaty that a president negotiated.

options.text: A simple majority of the Senate, followed by approval from both houses of Congress.
options.misconception: requires House approval of treaties as well

options.text: Two thirds of the full Senate membership, regardless of who is present.
options.misconception: confuses two thirds of members with two thirds present

options.text: Two thirds of the senators present and voting, followed by the president's signature.
A simple majority of each chamber, followed by approval from the Supreme Court.
options.misconception: adds a judicial approval step for treaties

questions.explanation: Ratification requires two thirds of senators present and voting, after which the president signs. The count is based on those present and voting, and no House or Court approval is part of the process.
questions.hint: Present and voting, then a signature.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the constitutional approval required before troops move into a war

stimulus.body: A chat digest relayed a popular blog claim that a president may order an invasion with no approval from anyone. The author added that the commander in chief clause covers deployments as well as declarations of war.

questions.stem: Slack digest SD-5 repeats a blog claim that 'a president may order an invasion with no approval at all.' What does the separation of powers require instead?

options.text: Presidential command of the forces and congressional approval of any troop funding.
options.misconception: reverses war and funding roles

options.text: A joint resolution approved by both chambers before any troop movement.
options.misconception: requires a joint resolution for any deployment

options.text: Presidential approval of congressional war powers before troops may move.
options.misconception: makes Congress depend on presidential approval

options.text: Congressional approval for the war and presidential command of the forces once authorized.

questions.explanation: The constitutional design splits the power: Congress decides whether there is a war, and the president directs the armed forces once that decision is made. The blog claim collapses both powers into the presidency.
questions.hint: Two powers, two branches.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Speaker cannot withhold a House-passed bill
questions.stem: Design critique asks the team to explain why the Speaker cannot refuse to send a House-passed bill to the Senate.

options.text: Sending passed bills onward is a constitutional duty, so refusal is not a discretionary tool.
Because the Senate could simply ask the House to send the bill again if it stalled.
options.misconception: invents a Senate subpoena power

options.text: Because the Speaker may be replaced by the House majority at any time.
options.misconception: treats the leadership as removable on demand

options.text: Because rules require the Speaker to send bills within twenty four hours.
options.misconception: invents a specific statutory deadline

questions.explanation: The Speaker's duty to send House-passed bills to the Senate is set by the Constitution and chamber rules, so withholding a bill is not an option the Speaker owns. Leadership power over scheduling does not extend to blocking a vote.
questions.hint: Is it a choice or an obligation?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the body that decides whether to impeach a federal judge
questions.stem: Audit item AU-22 asks which body can impeach and try a federal judge for misconduct.

options.text: The House holds the trial alone and removes the judge once the charge is sustained.
options.misconception: gives the House the role of the trial chamber

options.text: The House brings the charge, and the Senate holds the trial and decides on removal.
The Senate brings the charge and the House holds the trial before the president rules.
options.misconception: swaps the impeachment and trial chambers

options.text: A panel of senior federal judges tries the case and submits its verdict to Congress.
options.misconception: invents a judicial trial panel for impeachments

questions.explanation: Impeachment and removal are separate steps: the House charges and the Senate tries the case, with a two thirds vote required to convict. No judicial panel and no single chamber can do both jobs alone.
questions.hint: Charging and trying happen in different chambers.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the steps that end a filibuster in the Senate
questions.stem: Retrospective prompt asks the team to describe how a filibuster is ended and what the presiding officer does.

answer.exemplar: Once the required number of senators vote to end debate, the presiding officer of the Senate, normally the Vice President, declares that the debate is closed and moves the measure to a final vote. The action changes the schedule and leaves the senators to decide the bill's fate on that vote.

questions.explanation: Ending a filibuster is a scheduling act taken by a specified vote count. The presiding officer then moves the measure, and the outcome depends on the final vote rather than on the motion itself.
questions.hint: Who presides, and what happens next?

questions.learningObjective: Determine the outcome of a budget deadlock between the chambers
questions.stem: Planning ticket PT-4 asks what the House speaker must do when the House and Senate cannot agree on a budget.

options.text: Send the House budget to the Senate anyway and count it as the enacted budget.
options.misconception: treats one chamber's text as the final law

options.text: Call a joint session of Congress to settle the disagreement in one meeting.
options.misconception: invents a joint session for budget disputes

options.text: Adjourn Congress until the next year so the disagreement resolves itself.
options.misconception: assumes adjournment forces a resolution

options.text: Nothing beyond chamber procedure, because a budget deadlock simply means no budget law.

questions.explanation: A budget is a bill, so without agreement between the chambers there is no budget law. The Speaker's role is limited to chamber procedure, and neither a joint session nor an adjournment settles the disagreement.
questions.hint: No agreement means no enacted text.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the authority that must support a valid executive order

stimulus.body: The launch page tells customers that executive orders carry the force of law without any legislative vote, and that a signed order can settle any regulatory dispute in the company's favor. The page adds that no court review is needed beforehand.

questions.stem: Marketing blurb MB-8 claims that 'executive orders carry the force of law without any legislative vote.' Which principle makes that claim wrong?

options.text: Executive orders may only be issued during wartime emergencies declared by Congress.
options.misconception: restricts orders to wartime emergencies

options.text: An executive order must be grounded in a statute and cannot replace legislative lawmaking.
Executive orders must be countersigned by two members of the president's cabinet.
options.misconception: invents a countersignature requirement

options.text: Executive orders become permanent only after a confirming congressional vote.
options.misconception: requires a confirming vote for every order

questions.explanation: Executive orders operate within authority delegated by law; they are not a substitute for legislation. So the copy overstates the power, and its claim that no court review is needed also misstates how orders can be challenged.
questions.hint: Orders act inside the law, not instead of it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how courts resolve a conflict between state and federal law
questions.stem: Escalation note asks the team to explain how the courts resolve a conflict between a state law and a federal law.

options.text: The court picks whichever rule is more recent, no matter which level of government issued it.
options.misconception: applies a recency test across levels of government

options.text: The court applies the Supremacy Clause and the valid federal rule displaces the conflicting state rule.
The court sends the question to the state legislature for a clarifying amendment.
options.misconception: returns legal disputes to a legislature

options.text: The court applies the stricter rule so that no provision is ever violated.
options.misconception: believes courts pick the stricter of two laws

questions.explanation: Constitutional conflict rules are fixed: valid federal law is supreme, so the state rule yields and the federal rule governs. Judicial review is how courts confirm that a federal statute itself stays within the Constitution.
questions.hint: There is a fixed rule for conflicts.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the approvals a bill needs before it reaches the president
questions.stem: Throughput item TP-3 asks which chamber's approval is required for a bill to become law.

options.text: Only the House must approve a bill, and the Senate may act only after the House votes.
options.misconception: makes the Senate's approval unnecessary

options.text: Only the Senate must approve a bill, since it is the chamber that can amend it.
options.misconception: believes amendment power equals sole approval power

options.text: Both chambers must approve the same text before the bill can reach the president.
A single chamber must approve a bill twice before it reaches the president.
options.misconception: requires a double vote in one chamber

questions.explanation: Both chambers must approve identical text, and only then may the president consider signing it. The Senate's amendment power does not let it skip the House, and a single chamber cannot enact a bill alone.
questions.hint: Same text, both chambers.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why only the House may originate bills raising revenue
questions.stem: Onboarding checklist asks the team to explain why only the House may originate bills raising revenue.

answer.exemplar: The Constitution requires that bills for raising revenue originate in the House of Representatives, which was the chamber the framers tied most closely to popular election. The Senate retains the power to amend, delay, or reject such a bill, so the rule constrains where a revenue bill starts rather than eliminating Senate influence over it.

questions.explanation: The rule is a structural check on the taxing power, not a blanket removal of Senate power. It makes the elected lower chamber the starting point for revenue bills.
questions.hint: Start where elections are closest.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the legal effect of a ratified and signed treaty
questions.stem: Rollout item RO-2 asks which action follows a president's signature of a treaty that the Senate has already approved.

options.text: The ratified treaty becomes the supreme law of the land and binds the states as federal law.
The House must still approve the treaty before it binds the states.
options.misconception: adds a House step after presidential signature

options.text: The treaty must be published in the Federal Register before it takes effect.
options.misconception: treats publication as the condition of taking effect

options.text: The Supreme Court must confirm the treaty's constitutionality before it binds the states.
options.misconception: requires judicial confirmation of treaties

questions.explanation: Once the Senate ratifies and the president signs, the treaty is the supreme law of the land and binds the states. No further congressional or judicial step is part of the process.
questions.hint: What does a ratified treaty become?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the accurate element of a statement about war powers

stimulus.body: A draft article states that the president commands the army in wartime while Congress only supplies it, and it presents that division as the whole of the war power. It adds that approval for a war is a formality arranged after the fact.

questions.stem: Architecture article AA-10 states that 'the President commands the army in wartime; Congress only supplies it.' Which part of that is accurate?

options.text: The funding part, because Congress's real role in war is limited to paying for it.
options.misconception: denies Congress any role beyond funding

options.text: The commander part, because the president leads the armed forces as commander in chief.
Neither part, because the Constitution leaves all war powers to the states.
options.misconception: claims war powers were reserved to the states

options.text: Both parts, because war powers were deliberately split in two.
options.misconception: treats the division as if it were complete and correct

questions.explanation: The president does command the armed forces, so that half of the article is accurate. The error is reducing Congress to a funding role and dismissing approval after the fact, because the power to declare war sits with Congress.
questions.hint: Half right, half reduced too far.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the leadership role of the Speaker from an ordinary member's vote
questions.stem: Support ticket ST-6 asks the team to explain how the Speaker differs from a member who simply votes.

options.text: The Speaker votes twice on every measure, once as a member and once as presiding officer.
options.misconception: invents a double vote for the Speaker

options.text: The Speaker may rule any measure out of order without any possibility of appeal.
options.misconception: makes the Speaker's rulings unchallengeable

options.text: The Speaker presides over the House, sets its calendar, and represents the chamber in negotiation.
The Speaker holds the deciding vote whenever the House splits evenly on a question.
options.misconception: assumes the Speaker casts a tie breaking vote

questions.explanation: The Speaker is chosen by the House to preside, schedule, and speak for the chamber. That is a leadership role rather than an extra vote, and chamber rules allow the House to overturn a ruling.
questions.hint: Leadership is not an extra vote.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the remedy a federal court may use against an unconstitutional law
questions.stem: Governance item GV-13 asks what a federal court may do when a law conflicts with the Constitution.

options.text: The court may suspend the law until the president agrees to sign a revised version.
options.misconception: makes the president a reviewer of court rulings

options.text: The court may send the law back to Congress for correction before taking any further step.
options.misconception: assumes courts remand laws to Congress

options.text: The court may interpret the law so narrowly that it no longer conflicts with the text.
options.misconception: treats narrowing as the only remedy available

options.text: The court may refuse to enforce the law and hold the unconstitutional provision has no effect.

questions.explanation: Judicial review lets a federal court hold a law unconstitutional and refuse to enforce the conflicting part. The other answers describe powers courts do not have, though a court may of course interpret a statute narrowly.
questions.hint: Think about what the court refuses to apply.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare the vote needed to end debate with the vote needed to override a veto
questions.stem: Review checklist asks the team to explain why ending debate is easier than overriding a veto.

answer.exemplar: Ending debate needs only the number of senators the Senate rules require to vote for the motion, and that number has been lowered over time. Overriding a veto requires two thirds of the members present and voting in each chamber, which is a much higher bar and has to be cleared in two chambers at once.

questions.explanation: The two thresholds differ in size and in how many bodies must act. The motion to end debate is a single chamber decision made by a specified number, while the veto override needs supermajorities in both chambers.
questions.hint: Compare the counts and the number of chambers.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the legal effect of a stopgap funding measure
questions.stem: Handoff note HO-15 asks what becomes law when Congress passes a stopgap funding measure instead of a full budget.

options.text: The full budget is enacted once the stopgap measure is signed by the president.
options.misconception: treats a stopgap as automatic approval of the budget

options.text: The stopgap measure is enacted as an ordinary law and funds programs for a limited period.
Nothing becomes law because a stopgap measure lacks the force of a budget.
options.misconception: believes stopgap measures cannot be enacted

options.text: Only the stopgap measure is temporary in name while the full budget takes effect.
options.misconception: claims the budget follows the stopgap automatically

questions.explanation: A stopgap or continuing resolution is enacted through the same lawmaking path as any other bill, so it has full legal force for the period it covers. It buys time; it does not enact the full budget.
questions.hint: It is a bill like any other bill.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the constitutional bar to debt relief by executive order

stimulus.body: Changelog 2.4 lists a plan to cancel private student debt by executive order alone, with no action by Congress and no new statute. The entry notes that the plan was written after a legal review that accepted the president's general authority over economic affairs.

questions.stem: Changelog CL-3 notes a plan to 'cancel debts by executive order alone.' Which constitutional requirement defeats that plan?

options.text: Debt cancellation must be approved by every state where the borrowers live.
options.misconception: invents a state role in private debt relief

options.text: Executive orders about debt must be published in the official gazette before signing.
options.misconception: invents a gazette publication requirement

options.text: Congress controls spending and taxation, so debt relief needs legislation, not an order.
Only Congress may cancel debt, but an order may be issued to enforce an existing statute.
options.misconception: confuses enforcing a statute with creating debt relief

questions.explanation: Relief that costs the federal government requires an appropriation from Congress, so an order alone cannot do it. An order can enforce an existing law but cannot create new relief on its own.
questions.hint: Does it cost the federal government money?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the Supremacy Clause in resolving conflicting rules
questions.stem: Architecture decision AD-7 asks why the Supremacy Clause matters when two legal rules point opposite ways.

options.text: It gives the federal government the power to veto any state law at any time.
options.misconception: turns preemption into a federal veto power

options.text: It lets the president choose whichever rule serves national interests best.
options.misconception: hands the conflict to the president

options.text: It requires both levels of government to reach agreement before either rule applies.
options.misconception: makes conflicting rules wait for agreement

options.text: It makes valid federal law control over conflicting state law, resolving the conflict by rule.

questions.explanation: The Supremacy Clause supplies a deterministic rule for conflicts: valid federal law governs. That removes the need for bargaining between the levels of government whenever the two texts collide.
questions.hint: A rule, not a negotiation.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why confirmations are subject to Senate procedure
questions.stem: Hiring ticket HT-9 asks why most confirmations move through two chambers instead of one.

options.text: Nominations are Senate business, and the Senate's own procedures allow long delays before a vote.
Every nomination must also clear a House committee before the Senate will consider it.

options.text: Confirmations need the approval of both chambers because each claims joint foreign powers.
options.misconception: invents shared foreign powers in confirmation

options.text: The House and Senate must approve each nominee on the same day to avoid delay.
options.misconception: requires same day votes in both chambers

questions.explanation: The Senate confirms nominees, and its rules let majority members defer consideration as long as they hold the floor. The two step impression comes from appointments flowing from Senate advice and consent, not from a House vote.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the defect in a revenue bill introduced only in the Senate
questions.stem: Team quiz asks the team to describe what would happen if the Senate alone tried to originate a revenue bill.

answer.exemplar: A revenue bill introduced only in the Senate is defective under the origination clause, because the Constitution requires such bills to start in the House. The measure can be redrafted and introduced in the House, and then the Senate may take it up and act on it in the ordinary way with its usual powers of amendment and delay.

questions.explanation: The origination rule defines where a revenue bill must begin, and a bill that starts in the wrong chamber cannot be enacted that way. It constrains the starting point rather than removing the Senate's later role.
questions.hint: Wrong starting chamber means a defective bill.

options.misconception: borrows the amendment threshold for treaties

questions.explanation: Treaty ratification takes two thirds of senators present and voting, so the denominator is those voting on the question. A simple majority and the three quarters amendment threshold are both wrong.
questions.hint: Who is in the denominator of the fraction?

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a declaration must precede a war rather than follow it

stimulus.body: A spec being reviewed says the president declares war in one sentence and Congress objects later if it disagrees. The reviewer flagged that the sentence leaves the congressional role undefined and asked for a rewrite.

options.text: The president declares war but must notify Congress within a fixed number of days.
options.misconception: invents a notice deadline instead of prior approval

options.text: The sequence is fine because the declaration only takes effect after both houses vote.
options.misconception: assumes a later ratification step fixes the order

options.text: Only the Senate declares war, and the House must be notified afterward.
options.misconception: gives the war power to a single chamber

options.text: Congress declares war, so congressional approval comes first rather than after the fact.

questions.explanation: The constitutional sequence puts the declaration in Congress's hands, so Congress acts before the war begins. Saying the president declares and Congress objects later reverses the roles and the order.
questions.hint: Approval has to come before, not after.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Speaker is chosen within the House
questions.stem: Product question PQ-8 asks the team to explain why the Speaker is a member of the House who is chosen by the House.

options.text: Because the president cannot appoint anyone who has served in the House.
options.misconception: invents an experience requirement for the Speaker

options.text: Because the presiding role belongs to the chamber, which selects its own officer.
Because the Speaker serves for life once elected and cannot be replaced.
options.misconception: asserts the Speaker serves for life

options.text: Because the Speaker is chosen by a nationwide election held alongside House elections.
options.misconception: claims a separate national election for the Speaker

questions.explanation: The Speaker is an officer of the House chosen by its members, which keeps the role anchored in that chamber. The president, the Senate, and the electorate at large all play no part in the selection.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which bodies decide impeachment and removal of a federal judge
questions.stem: Legal ticket LT-12 asks which body decides whether to impeach and remove a sitting federal judge.

options.text: The Senate decides whether to charge and remove in one combined proceeding.
options.misconception: merges the impeachment and trial stages

The House decides whether to remove once the president requests the removal.
options.misconception: makes removal depend on a presidential request

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a vote to end debate accomplishes in the Senate
questions.stem: Demo prep asks the team to explain what a vote to end debate actually accomplishes in the Senate.

answer.exemplar: A successful vote to end debate ends the discussion and moves the measure forward, so the floor turns to the question of passage. It does not approve the bill and does not guarantee a final outcome, because the senators then vote on the measure itself, and that vote decides the result.

questions.explanation: The motion is a gate, not a verdict. What it changes is the schedule, and the later vote on the measure is what decides whether the bill passes.
questions.hint: A gate, not a verdict.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which chamber can block an appropriation the other chamber approved
questions.stem: Release blocker RB-6 asks which chamber's refusal can stop a budget the other chamber already approved.

options.text: The House, because the revenue origination rule gives it final control over spending.
options.misconception: confuses origination with final approval of spending

options.text: Neither chamber, because the president must approve every appropriation separately.
options.misconception: makes presidential approval a per-appropriation veto

options.text: Both chambers together, because a budget needs a two thirds vote in each.
options.misconception: raises the threshold for ordinary appropriations

options.text: The Senate, because an appropriation must be approved by both chambers before it becomes law.

questions.explanation: An appropriation is a bill, so approval in one chamber is not enough; the other chamber's refusal stops it. Ordinary appropriations need a simple majority, not supermajorities, and presidential signature follows rather than precedes.
questions.hint: An appropriation is a bill.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the principle that limits suspending a statute by order

stimulus.body: A planning memo proposes a system that suspends a statute the Senate passed whenever the president signs a memorandum. The memo reasons that the memorandum is a lawful exercise of executive authority because it comes from the president alone.

questions.stem: Planning memo PM-14 claims that 'an executive order can suspend a statute the Senate passed.' What principle limits that power?

options.text: An order must operate within existing statutory authority and cannot suspend a valid law.
A statute can be suspended only if the House agrees by a simple majority.
options.misconception: invents a House role in suspending statutes

options.text: A suspension order must expire at the end of the congressional term.
options.misconception: invents a term limit on orders

options.text: A suspension order is valid if the Supreme Court has not objected within a year.
options.misconception: treats silence as judicial approval

questions.explanation: Executive authority comes from law and operates within it, so an order cannot suspend a valid statute. The memo's reasoning would let the president repeal legislation without Congress, which the constitutional design does not allow.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why lower federal court rulings can be appealed
questions.stem: Compliance review CR-19 asks why a lower court's decision on a federal question can be appealed to a higher court.

options.text: Because any party may ask the Supreme Court to review any ruling in the country.
options.misconception: treats Supreme Court review as universally available

options.text: Because the court system is organized in tiers, so higher courts review decisions below them.
Because Congress can order retrials whenever it disagrees with a judgment.
options.misconception: gives Congress power to vacate judgments

options.text: Because state appellate courts sit above the federal trial courts in the same system.
options.misconception: puts state courts above federal trial courts

questions.explanation: A hierarchy of federal courts explains appeals: the decision of a lower court is reviewed by the court above it. That structure is distinct from judicial review of what a law means and from any congressional power over judgments.
questions.hint: Look at how the court system is built.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the second approval hurdle before a bill reaches the president
questions.stem: Estimating task ET-21 asks which approval step creates a second hurdle before a bill reaches the president.

options.text: Approval by the president, since no bill may be presented without a signature.
options.misconception: treats the signature as a pre-approval hurdle

options.text: Approval by the Supreme Court, since constitutional questions must be pre-cleared.
options.misconception: requires Supreme Court clearance of bills

options.text: Approval by a second chamber, since a bill must clear both the House and the Senate.
Publication in the Federal Register, since only published bills may be presented.
options.misconception: makes publication a precondition for presenting a bill

questions.explanation: The second chamber is the structural hurdle, since a bill must clear both House and Senate. The signature and any publication come after Congress has enacted the text.
questions.hint: Two chambers must agree on one text.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the revenue origination rule protects the public
questions.stem: Final checklist asks the team to explain how the revenue rule protects taxpayers from surprise tax hikes.

answer.exemplar: Because revenue bills must originate in the House, the chamber tied most directly to popular election, tax proposals begin where elected representatives are most accountable to voters. The rule slows the path to new taxes and gives the public a clearer chance to see and react to them before the Senate can act on a revenue measure.

questions.explanation: The rule changes the starting point for money bills, not the ultimate power, since the Senate still acts on them. Its design effect is added visibility and delay before a tax increase is adopted.
questions.hint: Visibility and delay are the design effects.
